summary: An informational RFC that recounts a discussion in the IETF DNS Working Group on load balancing, surveys other ways to provide or simulate it with the Domain Name System, and proposes a flexible approach for spreading load across servers.

plainLanguage.summary: If one shop is too busy, you could send some customers to its twin shop. This memo looks at ways for the Internet's phone book to point people at different servers to share the work.

questions: how can dns be used for load balancing
subtitle: Using DNS to distribute traffic across multiple servers.

tldr.problem: When multiple servers perform the same function, DNS needs a way to direct clients to different servers to share the processing load.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of modifying the DNS protocol, the solution uses custom zone transfer agents that reorder resource records based on server load, performance, or other metrics before distributing them.
tldr.outcome: This allows DNS to support load balancing without breaking backward compatibility, though it requires careful management of TTLs and refresh rates to stay accurate.

today: RFC 1794 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a reference for approaches to DNS load balancing without protocol modifications, though modern deployments often use other techniques like SRV records or external load balancers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1794 discusses how the Domain Name System can support load balancing by distributing requests across multiple servers. Rather than proposing changes to the DNS protocol itself, the RFC describes how existing DNS systems can be extended by making the zone transfer process smarter.

The goal is to maintain backward compatibility with all existing DNS implementations while allowing administrators to serve different addresses depending on server load, network conditions, or other factors.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's phone book (DNS) can point you to the least-busy server by sorting the addresses before handing them out.

sections.title: The Problem and History
sections.content:
The RFC recounts earlier approaches to load balancing in DNS. Early schemes included the "Shuffle Address" (SA) modifications, which randomly reordered address records, and round-robin methods that simply cycled through addresses in order. Later, some implementations used system load information to return addresses in order from least-loaded to most-loaded.

However, these approaches had drawbacks: they either ignored actual server load, required platform-specific system calls, or needed changes to the DNS specification itself. The DNS Working Group wanted a solution that met six criteria: backward compatibility, frequent updates, multiple addresses, proper interaction with other DNS records, flexibility for many types of load metrics, and fast calculation.
sections.plainLanguage: People tried different tricks to make DNS pick less-busy servers, but none worked well without breaking things or requiring special features.

sections.title: The Zone Transfer Solution
sections.content:
The solution leverages the zone transfer process, which DNS secondaries use to fetch updated records from primary servers. The RFC proposes making this process customizable by allowing administrators to specify a program to run during zone transfers.

Instead of a primary server sending records as they are stored, the zone transfer agent (a custom program) can read from any source—a load average daemon, configuration files, or other systems—and return records sorted according to those metrics. The records are presented to the nameserver for normal distribution to clients. For volatile zones with rapidly changing information, secondary nameservers can calculate the ordering themselves rather than relying on transfers from a primary, avoiding the problem of stale information during propagation delays.
sections.plainLanguage: The zone transfer (how secondary servers get updates from primary servers) can run a smart program that sorts the addresses by load before handing them out.

sections.title: Implementation and Performance
sections.content:
The RFC describes a working implementation in BIND that specifies a zone transfer program per domain. In practice, a script reads a list of addresses, randomizes their order, and inserts them into the zone file every 300 seconds (5 minutes). BIND has two limitations: it enforces a minimum TTL of 300 seconds and a minimum zone refresh rate of 15 minutes, both of which hamper volatile zones. The implementation works around this by lowering these limits to 60 seconds.

Performance testing on a Sun Sparc-2 showed that for one volatile zone with six address records refreshing every 300 seconds, BIND accumulated 64 seconds of CPU time over 24 hours—compared to 11 seconds with no fast zones. Refreshing every 60 seconds increased that to 5 minutes 38 seconds. The CPU load is linear with the refresh frequency, so administrators must balance the accuracy of load information against the cost of frequent updates.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can shuffle the addresses every 5 minutes to spread clients across servers. Faster updates use more CPU, so there is a trade-off between freshness and cost.

references.text: Mockapetris, P., "Domain Names - Implementation and Specification", STD 13, RFC 1035, USC/Information Sciences Institute, November 1987.
